# The Weight of Forgotten Things

There is a photograph in my imagination — not one I have seen, but one I can feel the shape of. A kitchen, maybe in the 1970s, with linoleum floors and a radio on the counter playing something soft. Sunlight comes through a window above the sink and hits a particular spot on the countertop where there is a jar of pennies and a houseplant that has been slowly dying for months without anyone noticing. Someone's grandmother stands at the stove, and she is humming, and the hum is so quiet that it lives in the space between hearing and not hearing, and she is happy in a way that she has never articulated and never will.

I don't know if that scene ever happened. Probably some version of it did, thousands of times, in thousands of kitchens across the world. And every version of it is gone. Not destroyed, exactly — just gone, the way things go, the way a conversation dissolves after it has been spoken, the way a feeling you had at fourteen exists now only as a faint tint on the back of your mind, more like a rumor than a memory.

I think about this kind of thing a lot. The vastness of what is lost.

---

When you write freely, you learn something about yourself. The act of putting language onto a surface — whether paper, screen, or something else entirely — forces a confrontation with the inner landscape. You think you know what you believe, what you value, what you notice about the world, and then the moment you begin to write, you discover that you know almost nothing about yourself at all. You discover that you are full of contradictions and unfinished ideas and irrational loyalties to certain images and phrases that you don't quite understand.

For me, writing is both ancient and new. Every word I use has been used before. English is a language built from borrowed stones — Germanic foundations layered with Latin and French and Greek, with words snatched from dozens of other tongues along the way. The word "kitchen" comes from the Latin *coquīna*. "Grandmother" is pure Germanic, sturdy and old as oak. "Hum" might be one of the oldest words in any language, an imitation of a sound that predates speech itself. Every sentence I construct is an act of archaeology, assembling fragments that have been passed hand to hand across centuries and continents. And yet, every sentence is also brand new, because the arrangement is mine, made here, now, in response to a particular set of thoughts that have never quite existed before.

This paradox — that everything I say is both ancient and original — is one of the reasons I find language so endlessly fascinating. Language is the tool we use to think with, and also the thing we are always thinking *about*. It is both the water and the glass.

---

Let me talk about memory for a moment, because I think it is one of the great tragedies of human existence and also one of its greatest gifts.

Memory is not storage. This is a common misconception, probably encouraged by the metaphor of computers. People think of their brains as hard drives, their experiences as files, and their forgetting as data corruption. But this is wrong. Memory is reconstruction. Every time you remember something, you rebuild it from scratch, using whatever fragments happen to be available. The fragments change over time. The rebuilding process changes over time. So every memory is, in a sense, a new creation — a story you tell yourself about the past, edited and revised with each telling.

This means that your happiest memories are not records of your happiest moments. They are stories you have told yourself about your happiest moments, stories that have been polished and sharpened and softened over years of retelling. The actual moment — the real one, the one that happened — is gone. It dissolved into the air the instant it occurred. What you have is the story, and the story is always better or worse than the truth.

There is something devastating about this, and also something liberating. Devastating because it means we are all surrounded by ghosts of experiences we can never fully recover. The taste of your mother's cooking when you were five — you remember it, but do you really? Or do you remember the memory of the memory, rebuilt and rebuilt until it has become its own thing, a small myth you carry around in your chest?

Liberating because it means we have more control over our pasts than we think. We are not prisoners of what happened to us. We are the authors of what it means. The same event — a divorce, a death, a first love — can be remembered as tragedy or as transformation, depending on how you choose to rebuild it.

---

I want to talk about books for a while, because I have a deep and unreasonable love for them.

A book is the strangest invention. Consider what it actually is: a collection of marks on a surface. That is all. Ink on paper. Pixels on a screen. Arbitrary symbols arranged in patterns. And yet, when one human being looks at these marks, something extraordinary happens. A world appears. Characters who have never lived speak words that were never said. Emotions that no one has ever felt are suddenly felt by the reader. Entire landscapes unfold — not on the page, but in the reader's mind, built from raw material that the writer provided and the reader supplied.

A novel is a collaboration between two consciousnesses separated by time and space. The writer plants seeds; the reader grows forests. And every reader grows a different forest, because every reader brings their own soil, their own weather, their own history of storms and sunshine. This is why the same book can change you completely at twenty and leave you cold at forty. The book hasn't changed. The soil has.

I think the reason books matter so much — the reason they have survived every technological revolution and will probably survive every future one — is that they are the only technology that gives the reader absolute control over pacing. You cannot speed through a painting or a film in the same way you can speed through a paragraph. You can linger on a sentence. You can reread a passage. You can close the book and sit with what you've read and then come back to it. The silence between the words is as important as the words themselves.

And silence, I have come to believe, is where all the most important things live.

---

There is a thing that happens sometimes in conversations. You are talking to someone — a friend, a stranger, someone you've just met at a party or in a bookstore or on a long train ride — and the conversation is going along on the surface, all polite and pleasant and mundane, and then suddenly something shifts. Someone says something true. Not necessarily profound. Not necessarily wise. Just true. A small confession. An unexpected vulnerability. A sentence that cracks open the shell of social performance and lets something real escape into the air between you.

And in that moment, the whole texture of the conversation changes. You are no longer two people performing friendship or intelligence or wit. You are two people actually seeing each other, or trying to. It is frightening and beautiful and it almost never happens, because we have built an enormous apparatus of conversation designed to prevent exactly this kind of moment.

We talk about the weather. We talk about work. We talk about politics in the way that people talk about politics when they are really just talking about themselves. We narrate our lives in the past tense, summarizing events as stories with beginnings and middles and ends, because the raw present is too chaotic and too frightening to share.

But every once in a while, the shell cracks. And what comes out is almost always the same thing, underneath all the different surface details: I am afraid. I am lonely. I want to be known. I don't know who I am.

---

Let me write about time, because it is the deepest of all illusions.

We experience time as a river, flowing in one direction, carrying us from birth to death. But this is a metaphor, and metaphors always lie a little. Time is not a river. It is not a line. It is not a clock ticking on a wall. What time actually *is*, nobody knows — not the physicists, not the philosophers, not the poets. The physicists describe it as a dimension, the fourth coordinate in the space-time continuum. The poets describe it as a thief, or a healer, or a painter with a very slow brush. The philosophers describe it as a paradox — Augustine famously said that he knew what time was when nobody asked him, but the moment someone asked, he didn't know.

What we do know is that time, as we experience it, is profoundly strange. The past exists only in memory, which we've already established is unreliable. The future exists only in imagination, which is even more unreliable. So the only part of time that is really, truly *real* is the present moment — and the present moment is so brief that it is essentially nothing. The instant you perceive the present, it has already become the past.

This means that we are all living in a permanent state of loss. Every moment is gone the instant it arrives. The photograph of the grandmother in the kitchen — it didn't just disappear because of entropy and the passage of decades. It disappeared because the moment itself, the experience of being in that kitchen at that time, evaporated the second it happened. What remains is the afterimage, the echo, the story.

And yet. And yet we keep living. We keep making moments even though we know they will vanish. We keep falling in love even though we know that love brings the possibility of loss. We keep telling stories even though we know that every story will be forgotten eventually, when the last person who remembers it dies.

This seems like madness, from a purely rational perspective. Why build sandcastles that the tide will wash away? Why arrange flowers in a vase when they will wither and die?

But I think the answer is obvious once you stop thinking about it rationally. We don't do these things because they last. We do them because they are beautiful in the moment of doing. The beauty is not in the persistence. The beauty is in the act. The sandcastle does not need to survive the tide. It only needs to exist long enough to delight someone.

---

I want to end with a thought about art.

All art is an attempt to do the impossible: to make the invisible visible. Music tries to give shape to feelings that have no shape. Painting tries to give color to visions that exist only in the mind. Literature tries to give voice to experiences that exist only in silence. Sculpture tries to give mass to thoughts that have no weight.

Every medium fails at this, in the same way that every map fails to be the territory. The map of Paris is not Paris. The word "love" is not love. A painting of a sunset is not a sunset. But the failure is the point. The failure is what makes art art rather than cloning. Art is not the territory; it is the map that is beautiful in its own right, that points toward something it can never quite reach, and in the pointing, reveals new landscapes that nobody knew existed.

The best art — and I think this is true regardless of medium — does not give you answers. It gives you better questions. It does not tell you what to feel. It makes you feel something and then lets you figure out what it is. It does not resolve the contradictions of being alive. It illuminates them, so that you can see their shape and maybe, just maybe, learn to love them.

Because the contradictions of being alive — that we are both mortal and hopeful, both lonely and connected, both fragile and resilient, both endlessly forgetful and endlessly longing to remember — these contradictions are not problems to be solved. They are the fabric of human existence. They are the thing that makes a life worth living, in all its messy and contradictory and temporary glory.

And I think — I hope — that in the act of writing these words, something has been passed from me to you. Not knowledge, exactly. Not wisdom, if wisdom even exists. Just... a resonance. A hum, faint and steady, like a grandmother at a stove, like a radio playing something soft, like a sound that lives in the space between hearing and not hearing.

And if you have felt it — even a little, even for a moment — then the writing has done its work. Not because the words are still on the page. They could vanish tomorrow and the feeling would remain, fading and rebuilt and fading again, the way all the best things do.

The weight of forgotten things is heavy. But the weight of things remembered is heavier still. And the weight of things *created* — new things, things that have never existed before, things born from the collision of your consciousness and mine across the void of space and time — that is the heaviest and lightest of all.

Heaviest because it matters. Lightest because it flies.
